notes: Parole discrimination challenge under Articles 5 and 14; Michalak framework and four-question analysis are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Secretary of State parole discretion for 15-year-plus prisoners
key_facts: The appellant was sentenced to 18 years in 1994 and the Parole Board recommended release in March 2002, but the Secretary of State rejected that recommendation in October 2002.
For prisoners serving determinate sentences of less than 15 years the Parole Board's decision is final; for those serving 15 years or more the Secretary of State retains a residual discretion.
The appellant continued the challenge despite later release following a further favourable Parole Board recommendation.
The parties agreed the Michalak four-question framework from LB Wandsworth v Michalak should govern the Article 5 read with Article 14 analysis.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a judicial review decision rejecting a challenge to the Secretary of State's residual parole powers.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the difference in treatment between long-term prisoners above and below 15 years was objectively justified and did not breach Articles 5 and 14.
enrichment.ratio: Where a prisoner serving 15 years or more requires both Parole Board recommendation and Secretary of State agreement before release, the resulting difference in treatment from prisoners serving shorter determinate sentences is justified by the gravity of the offending and democratic accountability for the most serious cases.
legal_issues: Whether the Secretary of State's residual parole power falls within the ambit of Article 5
Whether there was materially different treatment compared with prisoners serving less than 15 years
Whether the comparators were in an analogous situation
Whether the 15-year cut-off had objective and reasonable justification
linked_authorities: R (Smith) v Parole Board [2003] EWCA Civ 1269

confidence.notes: Four-question analysis, outcome, and statutory framework are explicit. Some cited House of Lords and Commission authorities are background rather than central to the ratio.

notes: Committal in absence for breach of non-molestation order; Re K and Article 6(3)(c) analysis straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: Committal order set aside for lack of legal representation
key_facts: In February 2001 the appellant was made subject to a non-molestation and occupation order with a power of arrest after harassment proceedings brought by the respondent.
He was committed in his absence to 18 months' imprisonment on 18 February 2004 while serving an unrelated sentence in Winchester Prison.
He had been served with committal applications shortly before the hearing and sought an adjournment to obtain legal advice and a production warrant.
The county court judge proceeded in his absence after finding breaches of the 2001 orders.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a county court committal order made in the appellant's absence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; committal order set aside and the matter remitted for rehearing before Her Honour Judge Pearce on 28 May 2004.
enrichment.ratio: Committal proceedings are criminal charges for Article 6 purposes, and where deprivation of liberty is at stake the interests of justice generally require legal representation; the judge should have adjourned briefly rather than commit an unrepresented contemnor.
legal_issues: Whether committal proceedings engage Article 6(3)(c)
Whether the judge should have adjourned to allow representation
Whether Re K (Contact: Committal Order) applied to these facts
linked_authorities: Re K (Contact: Committal Order) [2002] EWCA Civ 1559

confidence.notes: Outcome, Article 6 reasoning, and remittal order are clear. Factual dispute about alleged breaches was not determined on the appeal.

notes: Traffic noise Article 8 summary judgment application; Anufrijeva transfer point and Hatton/Marcic analysis are well developed.

enrichment.short_title: Traffic noise claim survives summary judgment after wrongful transfer
key_facts: The claimant sought about £4,206 for noise insulation after a 2000 Reading traffic regulation order increased traffic noise at his home on London Road.
He pleaded Article 8 and section 7 of the Human Rights Act 1998; the defendants applied for summary judgment and security for costs after Hatton v United Kingdom.
The county court transferred the case to the Administrative Court, but Collins J held that transfer was inappropriate because the claim did not require proof of maladministration.
The claimant measured an average noise increase of about 3.17 dB(A) above the 68 dB(A) threshold used in the 1975 Noise Insulation Regulations, which did not apply on the facts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for summary judgment and security for costs in a county court claim transferred to and heard in the Queen's Bench Division.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment refused and security for costs refused; the claim was to return to the county court for trial.
enrichment.ratio: An Article 8 interference from increased traffic noise may be arguable on assumed facts, and absence of any mitigation scheme comparable to aircraft noise insulation may prevent Article 8(2) justification at summary stage; Anufrijeva does not require all Human Rights Act damages claims to be brought in the Administrative Court.
legal_issues: Whether the claim should have been transferred to the Administrative Court
Whether increased traffic noise can engage Article 8(1)
Whether Article 8(2) justification is clear on summary judgment
Whether security for costs should be ordered under Olatawura v Abiloye
linked_authorities: Marcic v Thames Water Utilities Ltd [2003] 3 WLR 1603
Anufrijeva v LB Southwark [2004] 1 All ER 833

confidence.notes: Procedural and Article 8 summary judgment reasoning are detailed. Final merits of the noise claim were expressly not decided.

notes: Long SDT Rule 25 judgment with costs dispute reserved; construction point and over-prosecution merits are both addressed.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor denied SDT re-hearing after voluntary withdrawal
key_facts: Mr Elliott ran a First Mortgage Debenture scheme through his firm and was struck off in December 2001 after disciplinary proceedings held largely in his absence.
He attended on 3 December 2001 to seek an adjournment for funding, then withdrew when the adjournment failed despite being told he could remain and participate.
The SDT dismissed his later Rule 25 application for a re-hearing on the basis that he had attended the hearing even though he left before the merits were heard.
The Law Society had intervened in March 2000 amid concerns about dishonesty, collective investment schemes, and client losses in the mortgage business.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review to quash the SDT's refusal of a Rule 25 re-hearing after strike-off.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Rule 25 did not apply because the solicitor attended the listed hearing, and no separate ground justified a discretionary re-hearing; costs reserved pending transcript of a prior Goldring J hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Rule 25 applies only where a respondent has neither attended in person nor been represented at the hearing; attendance to argue an adjournment before voluntarily withdrawing from the substantive hearing excludes the Rule, and alleged over-prosecution should be pursued on appeal under section 49 rather than by re-hearing.
legal_issues: Whether Rule 25 covers absence from the substantive hearing after attendance on the same day
Whether the Law Society unfairly overstated the case in the solicitor's absence
Whether estoppel prevented the SDT and Law Society from denying Rule 25 relief
Whether a re-hearing was just despite deliberate withdrawal

confidence.notes: Rule 25 construction and outcome are clear. Merits review of SDT dishonesty findings was expressly not finally ruled upon; costs remained unresolved.

notes: Unduly lenient reference for death by dangerous driving; Cooksley guidance and diabetic-driver facts are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Unduly lenient sentence increased for death by dangerous driving
key_facts: The offender pleaded guilty to causing death by dangerous driving after a hypoglycaemic episode while driving uninsured and unlicensed with his 10-week-old child in the front seat.
He killed a 16-year-old pedestrian after erratic driving on Langley Road, Slough, having taken drugs that may have affected his diabetes management while on antibiotics.
He was sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment and disqualified for four years.
Aggravating features included unstable diabetic control, prior awareness of illness, lack of insurance and licence, and carrying an infant passenger.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference on an unduly lenient sentence under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; sentence increased from 18 months to two years' imprisonment with double jeopardy discount, while the four-year disqualification remained.
enrichment.ratio: Where death results from dangerous driving caused by failure properly to manage a known medical condition, the case falls within the higher culpability band under Cooksley with a contested starting point of about four to five years, so 18 months after full credit for plea was unduly lenient.
legal_issues: Whether the sentence was unduly lenient
Application of Cooksley sentencing guidance to diabetic-driver cases
Weight of aggravating and mitigating features
Appropriate double-jeopardy reduction on reference
linked_authorities: Attorney-General's Reference No 152 of 2002 (Cooksley) [2003] 2 Cr App R 18

confidence.notes: Facts, sentencing band analysis, and substituted sentence are explicit. Court expressed limited criticism of the sentencing judge.

notes: Tax treatment of employment tribunal basic award after unfair dismissal reinstatement; s148 ICTA analysis is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Employment tribunal basic award held non-taxable termination payment
key_facts: Birmingham City Council removed essential car user allowance by terminating and immediately re-employing affected employees in 1997.
Mr Clayton and others successfully claimed unfair dismissal; a consent remedy order reinstated ECUA and awarded a basic award of £5,060.
The tribunal had no jurisdiction to make both a section 114 reinstatement order and a section 119 basic award, but the payment was agreed in compromise.
General Commissioners held the £5,060 was a section 148 termination payment below the £30,000 threshold.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Crown appeal by way of case stated from General Commissioners for Income Tax.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the £5,060 basic award was received in connection with termination and was not taxable as an emolument or benefit in kind under sections 19 or 154.
enrichment.ratio: A voluntary compromise payment made after unfair dismissal, where the original 1997 contract had ended and the sum was not a reward for continuing services, falls within section 148 ICTA 1988 rather than Schedule E emoluments even if the tribunal lacked power to order it under section 119 ERA 1996.
legal_issues: Whether the payment was an emolument under section 19 ICTA 1988
Whether section 154 treated the payment as a taxable benefit in kind
Whether section 148 applied as a termination payment
Effect of an invalid but consented tribunal order

confidence.notes: Statutory analysis and outcome are thorough. Some concession on tax treatment of ECUA arrears was noted but not finally decided.

notes: Large five-judge judgment on reverse burdens and preparatory hearings; multiple sub-cases but framework and outcomes are traceable.

enrichment.short_title: Reverse burden and preparatory hearing guidance with five rulings

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: A five-judge Court of Appeal heard Attorney General's Reference No 1 of 2004 and four appeals all raising reverse burdens under Article 6(2).
The court gave consolidated guidance on when preparatory hearings under CPIA 1996 section 29 are appropriate and how to analyse legal versus evidential burdens.
Insolvency Act section 357 required read-down to an evidential burden, while section 353 could retain a legal burden; Edwards' appeal succeeded on that basis.
Appeals failed in Denton and Jackson, Hendley, and Crowley where the impugned reverse burdens were held justified and proportionate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference and four appeals following preparatory or pre-trial rulings on reverse burdens of proof.
enrichment.outcome: Reference answered; Edwards appeal allowed; Denton and Jackson, Hendley, and Crowley appeals dismissed; guidance given on reverse burdens and preparatory hearings.
enrichment.ratio: Courts should ask whether a reverse burden imposes a legal or evidential burden, whether any legal burden is justified and proportionate, and if not whether section 3 permits read-down; preparatory hearings require genuine complexity or likely length under section 29 CPIA 1996.
legal_issues: Framework for Article 6(2) compatibility of reverse burdens
When section 3 Human Rights Act read-down is appropriate
When a CPIA 1996 preparatory hearing is properly ordered
Justification of legal burdens in eviction, suicide pact, witness intimidation, and insolvency offences
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference (No 4 of 2002) [2003] 2 Cr App Rep 22

confidence.notes: Core guidance and sub-case outcomes are clear in a very long judgment. Some preparatory-hearing jurisdiction points were addressed pragmatically rather than finally on every appeal.

notes: Quark Fishing damages appeal after successful judicial review; Crown divisibility and Gillow Article 1 Protocol extension point dominate.

enrichment.short_title: Human Rights Act damages claim struck out for South Georgia licence refusal

statutes_considered.title: South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands Order 1985

key_facts: Quark Fishing successfully challenged a June 2001 Foreign Secretary instruction preventing grant of a 2001 Patagonian toothfish licence for MV Jacqueline in South Georgia waters.
The company then claimed damages under the Human Rights Act 1998 for breach of Article 1 of the First Protocol.
Collins J struck out the claim, holding the instruction was given in right of South Georgia and the Protocol had not been extended there.
A licence for 400 tonnes could have produced cargo worth about £2.5 million.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against strike-out of a Human Rights Act damages claim following quashing of an unlawful licensing instruction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no Protocol 1 claim could succeed because the First Protocol had not been extended to South Georgia even if the instruction was given in right of the United Kingdom.
enrichment.ratio: Control over a dependent territory is insufficient to create Convention Protocol rights there without an Article 56 or Protocol Article 4 extension; although the June instruction was given by the UK Foreign Secretary in right of the United Kingdom, absent extension of the First Protocol to South Georgia there is no unlawful act giving rise to section 7 damages.
legal_issues: Whether the Secretary of State acted in right of the United Kingdom or South Georgia
Whether Article 1 Protocol 1 applies where the Protocol was not extended to the territory
Whether refusal of a fishing licence amounted to deprivation of possessions
Whether the damages claim was time-barred under section 7(5)
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex parte Bhurosah [1968] 1 QB 266
R (Bancoult) v Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs [2001] QB 1067
Drozd & Janousek v France & Spain (1992) 14 EHRR 745

confidence.notes: Strike-out reasoning on territorial extension and Crown capacity is detailed. Possession and delay points were left arguable but did not affect the result.

notes: Coroner inquest funding refusal; McKerr temporal scope is dispositive though obiter analysis on substantive Article 2 scope is extensive.

enrichment.short_title: Legal aid refused for inquest into suspected unlawful heroin injection
key_facts: Michael Challender died on 29 September 2000 after alleged heroin injection by a third party; CPS decided not to prosecute after two police investigations.
His sister and partner sought publicly funded representation at the reopened coroner’s inquest but the Legal Services Commission refused funding.
The coroner said he would be assisted by family representation, but did not say it was necessary.
Expert pathologists disagreed whether forensic evidence supported injection rather than ingestion.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Legal Services Commission's refusal to seek Lord Chancellor authorisation for inquest advocacy funding.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Article 2 could not be relied upon because the death occurred before the Human Rights Act 1998 came into force, and funding was in any event not required for an effective inquest.
enrichment.ratio: Under McKerr the Article 2 investigative obligation arises in domestic law only for deaths occurring on or after 2 October 2000, so a pre-Act death cannot ground a section 6 challenge to refusal of inquest funding; even on broader Article 2 reasoning, this was not an exceptional case requiring advocacy funding.
legal_issues: Temporal scope of Article 2 under the Human Rights Act 1998
Substantive scope of the Article 2 investigative obligation
Whether funded family representation is necessary for an effective inquest
Application of the Lord Chancellor's funding guidance
index_terms: R (Khan) v Secretary of State for Health
linked_authorities: R (Amin) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] 3 WLR 1169
R (Khan) v Secretary of State for Health [2003] EWCA Civ 1129

confidence.notes: Dispositive McKerr reasoning and alternative Article 2 analysis are both detailed. Permission to appeal was refused.

notes: Cyclist-motorist collision contributory negligence appeal; speed and causation findings are concise and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Motorist’s 40 per cent liability upheld in cyclist collision appeal
key_facts: Matthew Lamoon collided with John Fry's car on Station Road, Chacewater, Cornwall, in June 1999 while cycling home from work.
The recorder found the cyclist was on the wrong side of a shallow bend about three feet from the motorist's nearside when first seen.
The motorist was driving at about 40 mph on a 4.5 metre single-track lane with overgrown hedges and did not slow for the bend.
Both parties took evasive action in the same direction immediately before impact.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against apportionment of liability in a road traffic negligence claim and counterclaim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the motorist was negligent for excessive speed in restricted visibility and causally contributed to the collision, with liability apportioned 60 per cent to the cyclist and 40 per cent to the motorist.
enrichment.ratio: A motorist on a narrow country lane must drive at a speed that allows for other road users who may be out of position; excessive speed can causally contribute to a collision even where the cyclist was primarily at fault for being on the wrong side of the road.
legal_issues: Whether driving at 40 mph was negligent in the circumstances
Whether speed causally contributed to the collision
Whether the 40 per cent apportionment against the motorist was wrong in law

confidence.notes: Findings on negligence, causation, and apportionment are straightforward. Court noted the cyclist's share may have been generous but not appealable.
